extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and law students working on patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of legal standards governing contributory and joint infringement and the personal and corporate liability rules (injunctions, recoveries of profits/damages, statutory liability) in patent suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — furnishing a part intended for assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person furnishes one part of a patented combination, intending that it shall be assembled with the other parts and that the complete combination shall be used or sold, that person is liable as an infringer of the patent on the complete combination; the part furnished must be an element of the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the part is sent abroad to be incorporated there, the sender may not be guilty. The supplier's intent/knowledge that the part is to be used in the patented combination is critical to liability; mere sale of a component that is capable of non-infringing uses may absolve the supplier absent knowledge or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — furnishing machines or articles especially adapted for infringing uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who furnishes a machine useful only for the purpose of making a patented article, intending that it shall be thus used, is himself liable for any infringement afterward committed in manufacture with that machine. Similarly, furnishing articles for that machine to operate upon, intending their use, or furnishing an article particularly adapted to be used in performing a patented process with the intent it be so used, creates contributory liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability hinges on intent/knowledge that the supplied item will be used in the infringing way. If the furnished machine or article is also useful for other lawful purposes and the supplier did not intend or know it would be used to infringe, there is no liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge/intent as defense when component has substantial noninfringing uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the property furnished is useful for some other purpose than to be a part of a patented combination or to perform a patented process, and the supplier does not intend or know when furnishing it that it is to be thus used, he incurs no liability for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of specific proof of knowledge or intent, the fact that the property could be used with non-infringing articles/machines and that many such non-infringing uses exist is sufficient to absolve the supplier from infringement. But proof of knowledge/intent defeats that defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller of old parts in combination-invention cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention consists merely of a new arrangement of old parts, one who sells the old parts is not chargeable with infringement unless they were sold with knowledge that they were intended to be used in making up the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge that the parts will be combined to recreate the patented combination is required to impose contributory liability on sellers of conventional parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of substitution / re-supply of replacement elements (Leeds & Catlin rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The license incident to purchase of a patented machine includes the right to preserve its fitness for use by replacing elements that are expected to be frequently worn out or replaced during the machine's life; the test is whether the element supplied is consumed in the ordinary use of the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court distinguishes replacement strictly to preserve fitness from supplying competing new elements to expand functionality. 'Operative ultimate tool' parts meant to be frequently replaced may be resupplied; beyond wear/breakage replacement (e.g., supplying alternative repertoires not intended as substitutes for worn parts) is not licensed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for contributing money to infringing enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who contribute money for the purpose of supporting others in infringing a patent are liable as infringers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial support aimed at facilitating infringement is treated as actionable participation in infringement (case citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of assignor and assignee when infringement continues after assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an infringer makes a voluntary assignment for the benefit of creditors and the assignee continues the infringement, both assignor and assignee may be sued jointly for infringement committed before and after the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuance of the infringing activity by the assignee creates joint liability; both periods of infringement are actionable against the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of corporation and receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation and its receiver may be joined as defendants for infringements begun by the company and continued by the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court may include both corporate entity and receiver where infringing acts span successive responsible parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor who requires manufacture of prior patented device — joint infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the owner of a patent that infringes an older patent licenses another to use his device and furnishes plans/drawings requiring the making of the device of the prior patent without procuring consent of its owner, the licensor is a joint infringer with his licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively enabling or directing manufacture of a device that infringes a prior patent (without consent) exposes the licensor to joint infringement liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint infringement — owners/operators and contractors/subcontractors
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one man owns and others operate an infringing machine, all are jointly liable. Likewise, where a contractor lets part of work to a subcontractor and, in prosecution of their parts, each infringes a patent, both are liable as joint infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint liability arises from cooperating roles that together accomplish the infringing act; plaintiffs may join such parties in suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure in suits involving joint infringers — pleading limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of several joint infringers is sued, the other one or ones may be admitted as joint defendants to help defend the suit. The bill should declare only on the joint infringement and not on individual infringements of the respective defendants, for the latter would be demurrable for multifariousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plead only the joint cause of action to avoid multiplicity and demurrer; procedural joinder rules apply to joint infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maker, seller, and user are not automatically joint infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker, the seller and the user of a patented machine, manufacture, or other article are not joint infringers of the patent thereon (i.e., mere maker and seller do not automatically become joint tortfeasors with the user).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the maker may be bound by an injunction obtained against the dealer which the maker has openly and avowedly supported, even if the maker was not a party to the record; the maker/seller may also be admitted to defend suits against dealer or user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention and defense by maker/manufacturer
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker may be admitted by the court to defend as a party to a suit against the seller, or the seller may be admitted to defend the user, when the user is sued for using the article sold to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pending the suit, if plaintiff does something that would terminate it (e.g., purchases all the business and goodwill of defendant), the manufacturer who intervened may dismiss the suit or assume the defense and try the suit on the merits despite absence of the original defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferee of assets may be brought in and subjected to injunction/accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where pending suit a defendant corporation transfers all its assets and goodwill to another corporation, the transferee may be brought into the suit by supplemental bill and subjected to the injunction order and accounting, at least if the transferee had openly and avowedly defended the original suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transferee is not necessarily bound by prior findings of law or fact fixing profits against transferor; liabilities relate to respective periods of ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnership liability for infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: A partnership is liable to an action for an infringement committed in the regular course of the partnership business by one or more partners or under orders; also liable for infringements committed outside the regular course if previously authorized or afterward adopted as the act of the partnership by all partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A manager employed by the partnership who infringes is a joint infringer with the partners; absent authorization/adoption, partnership not liable for acts outside regular business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of joint-stock associations and members
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint-stock association is similarly liable: each member may be held as an infringer for acts of infringement committed by the association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective entities other than traditional partnerships may incur member-level exposure for association acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private corporation liability for tortious infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Private corporations are responsible for infringements committed, authorized, or ratified by them under substantially the same rules that govern liability of natural persons: the corporation is liable for torts authorized by it and for torts done pursuant to any authority to act on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider officers, agents, and servants as possessing broad discretion; acts within the extensive range of corporate powers will bind the corporation. Agency can be exercised by another corporation; the principal is bound where the agent infringes in authorized pursuance of corporate business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation organized to infringe may be sued preemptively
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation organized for the purpose of conducting a particular business alleged to infringe a particular patent may be sued on that patent without waiting for the infringement to begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where corporate purpose is to engage in infringing activity, pre-infringement injunctive relief or suit is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of liability in patent cases (threefold)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of liability for infringements of patents: (1) liability to an injunction; (2) liability to a recovery of infringer's profits; and (3) liability to a recovery of patentee's damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different policies and rules apply to each category and they may be enforced differently against corporate actors and individuals connected with the corporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions can be enforced against corporate officers/directors/stockholders
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree for an injunction against a corporation can be made to equally restrain all the officers, directors and stockholders of that corporation from doing whatever the decree forbids the corporation to do; the injunction will extend to them even though they enter the employ of another who was not a party to the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts sometimes dismiss representatives from suits seeking injunctions when the plaintiff's motive is merely to impose litigation costs on those individuals. The doctrine does not protect individuals who use the corporation as a shield to continue personal infringement; such individuals may be sued separately. Officers who resign and continue infringing remain bound by the decree and punishable for violations; persons who take over an enjoined business and continue it in spite of knowledge of injunction are liable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority-owner corporation liability for subsidiary's infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation that owns the majority of the stock of a subsidiary and utilizes the latter as one of its manufacturing departments may be directly liable where the patent has been infringed by the subsidiary in the course of the business of the main corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control and utilization of the subsidiary's operations by the parent can establish direct liability for the parent for infringing acts of the subsidiary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of infringer's profits — limits on personal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: No person is liable to a recovery of infringer's profits except such profits as were made by himself; profits made by a joint infringer with him may be larger than his own but are not automatically recoverable from another person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers, directors, and stockholders ordinarily have no profits traceable to corporate infringement beyond dividends or salary. A court of equity will not ordinarily pursue individuals' assets to satisfy corporate infringer profits unless the corporation is insolvent and unable to respond, in which case dividends (but not fair compensation for services) may be reached to satisfy recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of patentee's damages — different principles and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability to a recovery of patentee's damages depends on different reasons than liability for infringer's profits; historical rules limited actions at law against officers/directors/shareholders but later decisions modified director liability — the question is compound and context-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of personal liability for patentee's damages requires careful analysis of whether the individual personally conducted or authorized the infringing conduct; this area is complex and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrongs divisible — commission vs omission for corporate representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrongs are divisible into wrongs of commission (an officer/director/stockholder who manages and directs infringement) and wrongs of omission (one who has power to prevent the corporation from infringing but omits to exercise that power). A person without personal power to cause or restrain the infringement is not chargeable with either sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability depends on whether the individual actively caused the infringing act or failed to exercise available control to prevent it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stockholders' limited personal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stockholders seldom have any power, merely as stockholders, to control the corporation's action in matters of detail like infringement of a particular patent; unless it is shown a stockholder possessed such control-power, common law will not impose liability for corporate torts on mere stockholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule of limited liability for stockholders applies: they are not liable for corporate debts or torts absent special circumstances showing control or ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' duties and standards — control, direction, and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers are charged with superintendence and control of corporate transactions and have a duty to refrain from directing infringements and to prevent agents and servants from committing infringements in prosecution of corporate business. If an officer directs a specific thing which turns out to be an infringement, he is likely personally liable; if omission to prevent infringement is due to gross inattention, the officer may be liable to the corporation for resulting losses, but a mere error of judgment generally will not create liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an officer, in pursuance of general authority, directs production of a machine that may be made to infringe or not, the officer is bound to ensure it is not made so as to infringe. Conversely, where a subordinate acts on his own without special orders, ordinarily the superior is not personally liable at common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directors' collective liability and minority protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors act collectively; where an entire board unanimously orders an action that constitutes infringement, the directors may be held personally liable. Members of a minority who voted against the action should not be held liable unless they afterwards adopt/ratify it or their gross non-attendance makes them chargeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere status as a director does not by itself create common-law liability for corporate torts; liability follows collective deliberate action or later ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory liability and choice-of-law (application of state law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many states have statutes making officers, directors, or stockholders personally liable under specified circumstances. Under § 721 of the Revised Statutes, the laws of the several states are to be regarded as rules of decision in trials at common law in federal courts where they apply, so state statutes will probably have the same effect in a patent suit in a United States court as in a state court action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State statutory provisions on corporate personal liability should be consulted because they may alter or augment common-law liability rules in patent litigation in federal courts.
